In the basement of a municipal building that smells permanently of wet wool and radiator dust, there is an archive of extinct noises. It isn’t open to the public, mostly because the public wouldn’t know what to ask for, and partly because the curator, a man named Julian who wears fingerless gloves even in July, hates explaining his filing system.

Photographs get all the glory when it comes to grief. People keep shoeboxes of faces, faded beaches, dogs squinting into the sun in 1984. Sight is greedy like that; it tricks you into thinking you can pin a moment to corkboard like a beetle. Sound is more honest. You cannot freeze a sound. The instant you pause it, it ceases to exist. To hear anything at all, you have to spend time with it—literal seconds of your own living heartbeats traded one-for-one with the ghosts on the tape.

Julian knows this. That is why his shelves are lined with wax cylinders, brittle magnetic reels, polycarbonate discs, and clunky gray flash drives labeled in cramped, obsessive ink.

Aisle Four holds mechanical extinctions. Here sits the heavy, iron-jawed *clack-chunk* of a railway ticket punch from 1952. Beside it is the frantic insect chatter of a room full of telegraph keys, followed by the metallic waterfall of a rotary phone dial spinning back into place—specifically, an avocado-green wall unit from a kitchen in Toledo, Ohio, whose spring had gone slightly slack on the nine. Further down is the banshee shriek and static handshake of a 56k dial-up modem negotiating entry into a vanished internet, and the crisp, decisive snap of a cassette player’s plastic door closing.

Aisle Seven is harder to walk down. It is weather and geography. There is a forty-minute recording of wind moving through an American chestnut forest before the blight took the trees—a distinctly broader, heavier rustle than oak or maple, though no one alive would recognize the difference on a walk today. There is the groan of a glacier in Iceland that finished melting during the second Bush administration. There is the evening chorus of frogs from a wetland in Florida that is now a strip mall featuring a mattress outlet and a nail salon.

Julian spends his Tuesday mornings on Intake. People leave boxes outside the heavy fire door, usually when clearing out the houses of dead parents who had weird hobbies. Ham radio operators, amateur ornithologists, lonely men who bought expensive microphones in the seventies just to have an excuse to stand quietly in rooms.

Today’s box is cardboard, softened at the corners like an old paperback, smelling faintly of pipe tobacco and cedar. Inside are six quarter-inch magnetic tapes in yellowed boxes. No dates. No locations. Only numbers written in blue grease pencil: *1* through *6*.

Julian threads Reel 1 onto the Studer deck. He flips the heavy toggle switch. The vacuum tubes warm up, emitting that faint, sweet smell of baking dust. He puts on his headphones—big, cracked leather cans that clamp over his ears like seashells—and presses play.

At first, there is only tape hiss, the warm snow of blank magnetism. Then, space opens up.

You can always hear the size of a room before anything happens in it. Every four walls hold a specific silence, shaped by plaster, curtains, floorboards, and ceiling height. This room is small, wooden, likely bare of rugs. Somewhere outside, muffled by single-pane glass, tires hiss on wet pavement. Not modern tires—narrower ones, moving slower.

Footsteps enter. Leather soles, slightly uneven; the person favors their left leg. A chair scrapes back. A match strikes—that sharp, sulfuric *skritch*, the miniature gasp of ignition, followed by a long exhale of breath.

For four minutes, nothing else happens. Whoever turned on the microphone simply sat down to smoke in the rain. Pages turn—newspaper, judging by the wide, dry crinkle, too big and clumsy to be a book. A porcelain cup sets down onto a saucer with a tiny, flawed clink.

Then, from another room down a hallway, a woman’s voice calls out. The words are blurred by walls, reduced to pure melody—two rising notes, a question. Maybe *More coffee?* Maybe *Did the mail come?* Maybe *Are you coming back to bed?*

The person near the microphone doesn't shout back. Instead, the chair creaks, the footsteps return, moving briskly toward the door, eager enough that the slight limp turns into a tiny, syncopated hop. And then the room is empty again, left with the ticking of a wall clock and the rain, while the tape keeps faithfully turning, eating up thirty more minutes of nobody being there at all.

Julian stops the reel. He sits for a long moment in the amber glow of the level meters.

Historians want speeches. They want the roar of rockets lifting off from Cape Canaveral, crowds screaming in Berlin, prime ministers clearing their throats before declaring war. Those tapes are kept uptown, in marble buildings with climate control budgets and security guards.

Nobody asks for the sound of a person abandoning a cigarette to go answer someone they love in the next room. Yet Julian thinks if aliens ever pull the charred black box of Earth out of the cosmic wreckage, the speeches won't tell them anything useful. This will. The scrape of the chair. The hurry in the limp. The way two people shared a house on a wet morning and didn't know they were living inside the golden age of their own lives.

He pulls an index card from his desk drawer, uncaps his fountain pen, and thinks carefully before writing: *Unidentified domestic interior. Rain. Question asked; answered off-mic.*

At five o'clock, Julian locks the basement and climbs the concrete stairs to the street. Evening traffic grinds past. An electric car slides by making its artificial spaceship hum. A teenager’s phone bleats a three-note chime. Two pigeons argue on an awning. Julian takes off his gloves, closes his eyes, and listens to it all vanish.
